extracted.intended_audience: New York Times newsroom staff, editors, managers, and product/strategy teams
extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom strategy and standards report recommending how The New York Times should change its reporting, staffing, editing and product practices to become a subscription-first, digitally native destination. Focuses on story forms, visuals, training, hiring, organization, metrics and audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription-first business
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times is a subscription-first business; its incentives and strategy should prioritize acquiring and retaining subscribers rather than maximizing pageviews or low-margin advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means producing journalism that several million people are willing to pay for, aligning newsroom decisions with long-term subscriber value rather than short-term traffic. The report contrasts subscription-first incentives with the pageview/advertising arms race and frames subscriber value as the central metric guiding choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism worth paying for
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories must clear a bar of being 'journalism worth paying for' — distinctive, high-value reporting that is not easily replicated by free competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'dutiful' incremental news pieces that add little context or visuals and are undifferentiated from competitors. Prioritize impact, originality, reporting depth (profiles, investigations, long-form) and forms that expand readers' understanding. Evaluate whether coverage is 'so much better than the competition' that readers will pay for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the report more visual
rubrics_metrics.description: The daily report needs to become more visual; too much remains dominated by long strings of text and lacks embedded visuals that clarify and engage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand the number of visual experts and leadership roles, train reporters/critics to embed visuals contextually, let photographers/videographers/graphics editors lead some stories, and improve tools (e.g., Oak) and workflows so visuals are integrated early. Examples & anti-patterns: reader complaints about missing maps; stories that could be stronger with a graphic but get no help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a digitally native mix of journalistic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt and expand storytelling formats that fit digital habits — morning/evening/live briefings, email newsletters, alerts, FAQs, scoreboards, audio, video and other native forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these formats as part of core journalism (not side projects). Encourage a less institutional and more conversational writing style appropriate to these forms, remove bottlenecks to launching features, and involve more journalists in creative and production processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: New approach to features and service journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Reimagine features and 'guidance' journalism to make big digital bets in areas where The Times has competitive advantage, prioritizing service journalism that gives useful, actionable advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build modern versions of the 1970s features expansion (e.g., Cooking, Watching). Expand service offerings (guides, product collaborations like Wirecutter, Smarter Living) while continuing some traditional features that serve loyal readers. Be ambitious in devoting newsroom resources to new areas to attract subscribers and advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers must become a bigger part of the report
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase reader engagement and community features so readers feel part of a community and invest time on the Times platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand constructive commenting and discussion beyond current 'nooks and crannies' (Opinion’s The Stone, Wordplay, Well, Cooking). Use engagement to drive loyalty and network effects; create more opportunities for readers to interact, contribute and learn from each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand newsroom training
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantially expand training to give reporters and editors the skills needed to create digitally native journalism and use new storytelling tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make training systematic (not haphazard), start as soon as feasible, enable staff to maneuver across platforms and produce multimedia work. Training should let staff combine reporting expertise with new tools for visuals, audio, video and interactive formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accelerate hiring of top outside journalists and creators
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase the pace and focus of hiring to bring in visual journalists, reporters with unmatched beat authority and strong writing skills, and backfield editors who sharpen ideas and shape analytical, conversational stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize hires that move the newsroom away from print-focused roles toward multimedia-focused roles (senior visual journalists, reporters, graphics editors, photographers, producers). Hiring should increase even if it requires turnover and budget adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make newsroom diversity a top priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase diversity across the newsroom—more people of color, more women, journalists from outside major metro areas, more younger journalists and more non-Americans—to produce a richer report and to attract broader audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat every open position as an opportunity to improve diversity; extend efforts beyond recruiting to career development and mentorship; ensure leadership and coverage teams reflect the audiences sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rethink freelance strategy (expand and shrink selectively)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be more strategic about freelance work: expand freelance in high-value areas and eliminate or reduce low-value freelance spending in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that freelance often produces highly read and cost-effective journalism (Op-Eds, Op-Docs, Magazine pieces), but avoid across-the-board cuts. Conduct a rigorous review to decide which freelance work to increase, keep, or eliminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reorganize the newsroom for the digital present
rubrics_metrics.description: Reorganize structures, processes and rhythms that still reflect print legacy so the newsroom becomes more nimble, risk-taking and digital-first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce print-dominant scheduling constraints, create subject-focused teams (e.g., climate, gender), make the print hub more autonomous, and redesign desks so high-priority areas are not spread across multiple teams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every department should have a clear, widely understood vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Each department must articulate and communicate a clear vision covering what it will cover, who its audience is, and how it will operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective vision spans three areas: Journalism (coverage and forms and differentiation), Audience (target audience, how they find and consume coverage, what success looks like), and Operations (skills needed, staffing balance, interactions with print hub and cross-department teams). Departments should decide what to do and what not to do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set goals and track progress with accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Teams should set tangible goals, use data to track success, and be accountable—expanding teams that thrive, reallocating resources away from failing teams, and changing leadership when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use data (beyond single metrics), set targets (even rough ones) as focusing mechanisms, improve transparency about newsroom goals, and connect targets to resource and personnel decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redefine success beyond pageviews; measure subscriber value
rubrics_metrics.description: Pageviews are meaningful but insufficient; The Times needs a more sophisticated metric (and mix of metrics) that measures an article’s value in attracting and retaining subscribers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support efforts like the data and audience insights group's metric for subscriber value; balance quantitative measures with qualitative judgments, recognizing no metric is perfect. Prefer stories that make readers feel they got unique reporting even if not the most viral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize conceptual, front-end editing over low-value line-editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Shift editing resources toward front-end conceptual editing—sharpening story form, focus and newsgathering—while preserving rigorous copy-editing for spelling and grammar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce time spent on low-value line edits (moving/removing paragraphs) and increase editor time on shaping stories early in reporting. This will require changes across copy desk, backfield and masthead workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen collaboration between newsroom and product teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and product teams (product managers, designers, developers) should work more closely to create reading experiences as compelling as the journalism itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase mutual understanding of priorities and constraints, involve editors in platform experience planning, and align short-term newsroom needs with longer-term product visions. Example: homepage design and functionality have been static; better collaboration can improve this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce print's dominant role while improving the print product
rubrics_metrics.description: Decrease the extent to which print rhythms dictate newsroom organization and daily work, while making the printed newspaper even better via a stronger print hub.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a more muscular, autonomous print hub to free desks from print scheduling constraints, enabling subject-focused teams and better digital workflow. Preserve the print product as a curated version of best work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do fewer dutiful 800-word incremental stories; favor varied forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut back on routine 800-word 'dutiful' pieces that perform poorly online and produce more varied journalistic forms—profiles, investigations, long-form narratives, quick explainers, lists and live blogs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage reporters to choose appropriate forms for their stories; give field reporters the tools and authority to pick formats (e.g., launch a Facebook Live) without bureaucratic bottlenecks. Kill ideas that don't rise to memorable levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage versatility and hybrid roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with hybrid jobs (reporters who edit, editors who write) to flatten hierarchy, diversify skill sets, and encourage shared responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote movement between roles, create player-coach models, and evaluate editors on collaboration across desks. Make it easier for reporters to write across the paper and for enterprise editors to place work where it best fits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed visual expertise in pods/desks and make visuals accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Each reporting pod/desk should have a graphics/interactive/video point person involved from the start, and tools should make simple charts/maps easy for reporters to create.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involve visual staff at the beginning of reporting to identify stories ripe for media, reduce permission barriers ('special keys') for simple visuals, and accept a range between polished and intimate/serendipitous work appropriate for the internet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a more conversational tone where appropriate, with guardrails
rubrics_metrics.description: Use less institutional, more conversational writing to build loyalty and connection, while maintaining high standards to avoid tonal mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loosen rigid style where it helps engagement but ensure copy desks preserve accuracy and quality; recognize the Times is held to high standards and errors or tonal falsehoods can cause strong backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and use sophisticated audience metrics alongside qualitative judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Create and use better audience-insight tools (beyond pageviews) to understand what resonates, while accepting that metrics must be balanced with newsroom judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include a metric for article value to attracting/retaining subscribers. Provide broader access to data (not just narrow slices) so desks understand what success looks like and can make informed decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold leaders accountable to stated priorities and measurable targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders should be held accountable for executing priorities and meeting measurable targets (e.g., visual proportion of stories), and these targets should influence resourcing and personnel decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make priorities transparent and enforceable; don't allow long multi-year 'figuring it out' horizons—be willing to shift resources or change leadership when teams underperform.
